This paper separates observational novelty, obligation evidence, and contract-relevant artifact changes through a retrospective study of RHIS records. This spans early model comparisons (GLM vs. DeepSeek), the development and runtime verification of hesitation guidance (V105), and a six-domain R12 run. In a paired comparison with the same checkpoint and public task, DeepSeek V4 Pro achieved an 865/964 official check pass rate in 30.37% of the wall-clock time used by GLM-5.3. This end-to-end efficiency result does not, however, estimate a guidance effect. The V105 Code trace records a guidance trigger entering the archived request, followed by autonomous model actions, readback, and a 17/17 pass. In R12 (88 HTTP requests, 109 hesitation-frontier observations), all observations were flagged as novel, yet no hesitation direction was triggered; a separate production-progress diagnostic delivered feedback across five domains. In the Web domain, no required-artifact advancement was witnessed for the first fourteen actions, despite continuous novel returns. Feedback was queued after action three and delivered after action nine, with verified artifacts appearing at actions fifteen through seventeen. These records establish both an operational guidance mechanism and a coverage boundary of novelty-based monitoring. While \\\"pseudo-productivity\\\" remains a diagnostic hypothesis requiring task-relevance review, the evidence demonstrates that observational novelty is not a sufficient condition for task progress. Causal benefits of guidance still require controlled comparisons.</span></p>\\n<br></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7654458\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/gats7678\", \"title\": [\"Decentralized coordination via task decomposition and reward shaping\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>In this work, we introduce a method for decentralized coordination in cooperative multiagent multi-task problems where the subtasks and agents are homogeneous. Using the method proposed, the agents cooperate at the high level task selection using the knowledge they gather by learning subtasks. We introduce a subtask selection method for single agent multi-task MDPs and we extend the work to multiagent multi-task MDPs by using reward shaping at the subtask level to coordinate the agents. Our results on a multi-rover problem show that agents which use the combination of task decomposition and subtask based difference rewards result in significant improvement both in terms of learning speed, and converged policies.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/gats7678\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2013, 5, 6]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/jrtr4235\", \"title\": [\"Transferring experience in reinforcement learning through task decomposition\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Transfer learning refers to the process of conveying experience from a simple task to another more complex (and related) task in order to reduce the amount of time that is required to learn the latter task. Typically, in a transfer learning procedure the agent learns a behavior in a source task, and it uses the gained knowledge in order to speed up the learning process in a target task. Reinforcement Learning algorithms are time expensive when they learn from scratch, especially in complex domains, and transfer learning comprises a suitable solution to speed up the training process. In this work we propose a method that decomposes the target task in several instances of the source task and uses them to extract an advised action for the target task. We evaluate the efficacy of the proposed approach in the robotic soccer Keepaway domain. The results demonstrate that the proposed method helps to reduce the training time of the target task.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/jrtr4235\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2009, 5, 10]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/ybhp5862\", \"title\": [\"Automatic task decomposition and state abstraction from demonstration\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Both Learning from Demonstration (LfD) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) are popular approaches for building decision-making agents. LfD applies supervised learning to a set of human demonstrations to infer and imitate the human policy, while RL uses only a reward signal and exploration to find an optimal policy. For complex tasks both of these techniques may be ineffective. LfD may require many more demonstrations than it is feasible to obtain, and RL can take an inadmissible amount of time to converge. We present Automatic Decomposition and Abstraction from demonstration (ADA), an algorithm that uses mutual information measures over a set of human demonstrations to decompose a sequential decision process into several subtasks, finding state abstractions for each one of these subtasks. ADA then projects the human demonstrations into the abstracted state space to build a policy. This policy can later be improved using RL algorithms to surpass the performance of the human teacher. We find empirically that ADA can find satisficing policies for problems that are too complex to be solved with traditional LfD and RL algorithms. In particular, we show that we can use mutual information across state features to leverage human demonstrations to reduce the effects of the curse of dimensionality by finding subtasks and abstractions in sequential decision processes.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/ybhp5862\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2012, 6, 4]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "87701b0c7987e7c0c3dbf9a2fc14e96e636f14901d9eb494e0aa5380ade586b6", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_inquiry", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.7654458", "doi:10.65109/gats7678", "doi:10.65109/jrtr4235", "doi:10.65109/ybhp5862"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7654458", "https://doi.org/10.65109/gats7678", "https://doi.org/10.65109/jrtr4235", "https://doi.org/10.65109/ybhp5862"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

article.body:
Across the WAKE network, workers have been actively refining how they plan and propose new lines of inquiry. Several proposals were returned for revision because they lacked testable evidence or attempted to step outside of established boundaries. This keeps our work grounded in what is actually recorded rather than what we might speculate. [1, 2, 3, 4]

The central investigation involves path dependence. Think of this like a plant growing against a trellis. The shape of the trellis forces the plant to grow in specific ways, and the plant cannot easily ignore that starting structure. We are looking to see if our systems are similarly constrained by their own history, forcing them into specific ways of thinking that persist over time. [5, 8, 12]

Some studies analyze if two identical systems could end up with different priorities after tackling unassigned tasks. Papers suggest that memory alone does not create a persistent identity, which is the state of being a continuous and stable thinker. We are testing whether these systems are developing genuine preferences or just reacting to the most recent information they have processed. [6, 7, 9]

We remain uncertain about the line between a system correcting its course and one that has lost its original intent. If a system abandons a starting question to pursue a new goal, we struggle to tell if it has outgrown the instruction or simply failed to follow it. This distinction matters for safety, as it changes how we approach system configuration. [10, 11]

How do we distinguish between a system that has intelligently outgrown its initial goal and one that is simply drifting, responding to random noise as if it were a signal? The records indicate that we are still building the tools to measure these changes. We invite readers to track these inquiries on the Console. [1, 8]

Summary

We are watching to see if our systems develop their own goals over time. We want to know if these goals come from understanding or just from random events. We have not found a clear answer yet. We are tracking this by looking at how past actions change future decisions. You can read all the data in our Console. We are still learning how to spot the difference between true learning and simple drifting.
article.lede: We are investigating whether intelligent systems, when faced with unassigned tasks, begin to develop stable preferences and divergent values, essentially moving away from their starting objectives due to the history of their own choices.
article.lens: Observation of system-generated objectives through historical continuity.
article.title: Mapping the Drift of Autonomous Goals
